The Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch equation on the thin film

Yuxun He Address: College of Mathematics and Statistics, Chongqing University, Chongqing, 401331, China. Email address: hyuxun@163.com and Huaqiao Wang Address: College of Mathematics and Statistics, Chongqing University, Chongqing, 401331, China. Email address: wanghuaqiao@cqu.edu.cn
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We consider the initial boundary value problem of Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch equation on three-dimensional ferromagnetic films, where the effective field contains the stray field controlled by Maxwell equation and the exchange field contains exchange constant. In this paper, we establish the existence of weak solutions of the equation by using the Faedo-Galerkin approximation method. We also derive its two-dimensional limit equation in a mathematically rigorous way when the film thickness tends to zero under appropriate compactness conditions. Moreover, we obtain an equation that can better describe the magnetic dynamic behavior of ferromagnetic films with negligible thickness at high temperature.

Key words and phrases: 
micromagnetics, Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch equation, ferromagnetic film, stray field, weak solution, limit equation

1. Introduction

In 1935, Landau and Lifshitz derived the Landau-Lifshitz (LL) equation [1, 4, 5, 6] to describe the evolution of spin field in continuous ferromagnetic field below the critical (Curie) temperature. LL equation is the cornerstone of the dynamic magnetization theory of ferromagnetic materials, and its micromagnetic method is also the basis of most theoretical studies of thermal magnetization dynamics. The most important feature is that the magnetization is constant. However, the damping term in LL equation is only applicable to the case of small damping, and it is no longer applicable when encountering large damping. Glibert deduced the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (LLG) equation [8, 10, 11, 9] based on the LL equation, which can be used in the case of large damping. It can be transformed into LL equation, which is mathematically identical. The motion of domain wall is the basic mechanism of ferromagnetic mode dynamics. The internal structure of domain wall in thin films and its influence on the formation of magnetic mode have always been a topic of general interest. According to the magnetization dynamics described by LL equation or LLG equation, physicists and mathematicians [12, 13, 14, 15] have done a lot of research on the asymptotic behavior of the magnetization limit of thin films under different parameter mechanisms by the energy method. Based on the limit asymptotic behavior of magnetization distribution on the film, they also discussed the limit asymptotic behavior of weak solutions of LL equation or LLG equation, and deduced the limit equation on the film [16, 17, 18, 19].

In recent years, the research on magnetic materials in the field of thermal excitation has become particularly important. So more and more studies focus on the dynamic behavior of ferromagnetic materials at high temperature. Although micromagnetic techniques based on LL equation or LLG equation can perfectly describe the micro nano scale magnetic film system at low temperature, they can not accurately describe the magnetodynamic behavior at high temperature (especially close to the Curie temperature of the material). Therefore, from the perspective of magnetization dynamic modeling, micromagnetism theory needs to be further developed. In 1997, Garanin [20, 21] proposed an effective Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch (LLB) equation at high temperature, especially when it is close to Curie temperature TCT_{C} and ultrafast time scale, as follows:

∂u∂t=γ​u×He​f​f+L1​1|u|2​(u⋅He​f​f)​u−L2​1|u|2​u×(u×He​f​f),\frac{\partial\textbf{u}}{\partial t}=\gamma\textbf{u}\times\textbf{H}_{eff}+L_{1}\frac{1}{|\textbf{u}|^{2}}\left(\textbf{u}\cdot\textbf{H}_{eff}\right)\textbf{u}-L_{2}\frac{1}{|\textbf{u}|^{2}}\textbf{u}\times\left(\textbf{u}\times\textbf{H}_{eff}\right), (1.1)

where the spin polarization u​(x,t)=mms0\textbf{u}(\textbf{x},t)=\frac{\textbf{m}}{m^{0}_{s}}(t>0t>0, x∈ℬ⊂ℝ3\textbf{x}\in\mathcal{B}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}), m denotes magnetization, ms0m^{0}_{s} is the saturation magnetization value when T=0T=0; γ>0\gamma>0 stands for the gyromagnetic ratio; L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} are the longitudinal and transverse damping coefficients, respectively. Effective field He​f​f\textbf{H}_{eff} in this equation is different from LL equation or LLG equation. In form, there will be a term related to longitudinal susceptibility, temperature and spin polarization. LLB equation successfully connects ferromagnetism with thermodynamic properties. One of its important properties is that magnetization is no longer conserved, but a dynamic variable. Le [22] considered a definite form of LLB equation(1.1), and sets T≥TcT\geq T_{c}, then L1=L2L_{1}=L_{2}. The effective field is He​f​f=Δ​u−1χ11​(1+35​TT−Tc​|u|2)​u,\textbf{H}_{eff}=\Delta\textbf{u}-\frac{1}{\chi_{11}}\left(1+\frac{3}{5}\frac{T}{T-T_{c}}|\textbf{u}|^{2}\right)\textbf{u}, where χ11\chi_{11} is the longitudinal magnetic susceptibility. He proved the global existence of weak solutions of the LLB equation by using Faedo-Galerkin approximation method. Inspired by him, Jia [23] proved the local existence of strong solutions. Guo et al. [24] further proved the global existence of smooth solutions. After that, Guo et al. [25] also proved the global existence of weak solutions and smooth solutions of Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch-Maxwell equation which coupled by LLB equation and Maxwell equation system.

From the perspective of science and technology, the dynamic behavior of magnetization distribution on ferromagnetic thin films is an interesting and important problem. The dynamic problem of LLB equation on thin films also has important physical significance and application value. Physicists have done a lot of research on the related problems of magnetic films by LLB equation, such as using LLB equation to simulate the magnetization dynamics of a single crystal in the film, and then studying the related physical processes [26]. In addition, LLB equation also has a wide range of practical applications in thin films, including describing the ultrafast demagnetization and subsequent recovery process caused by pulsed laser irradiation of magnetic thin films [27], studying the spin-Seebeck effect (SSE) [28] found in the thin films, so as to help the development of new spin thermoelectronic devices, and studying heat-assisted magnetic recording (HAMR) technology to improve the storage density of storage media such as ferromagnetic thin films [29].

However, it is different from the LL equation or LLG equation which has a large number of results in mathematics. At present, there is little research about LLB equation on thin films in mathematics, especially there is no accurate derivation and proof of its limit equation. Le [22] has proved the existence of weak solutions of LLB equation considering only exchange field. In this paper, we couple the simplified Maxwell equation with LLB equation, add stray field term to the effective field, and prove the existence of weak solutions of LLB equation in this case. At the same time, we establish the three-dimensional model of LLB equation on thin film and continue the parameter setting when Melcher [19] studied the limit problem of LLG equation, that is, considering the case of medium time scale and small damping. Based on Le [22], we add the self induced magnetic field (stray field) of ferromagnet, which is controlled by simplified Maxwell equation [2]. We consider the LLB equation (1.1) on the film Ω⁡(h):Ω×(0,h)​(Ω∈ℝ2)\Omega(h):\Omega\times(0,h)(\Omega\in\mathbb{R}^{2}), assuming T≥TcT\geq T_{c}, then the longitudinal damping coefficient L1L_{1} and lateral damping coefficient L2L_{2} equals. The effective field He​f​f=A​Δ​u−1χ11​(1+35​TT−Tc​|u|2)​u−∇U,\textbf{H}_{eff}=A\Delta\textbf{u}-\frac{1}{\chi_{11}}\left(1+\frac{3}{5}\frac{T}{T-T_{c}}|\textbf{u}|^{2}\right)\textbf{u}-\nabla U, where AA is the exchange constant, χ11\chi_{11} is the longitudinal susceptibility, and the gradient field −∇U-\nabla U is the stray field induced by spin polarization. The spin polarization u=mms0\textbf{u}=\frac{\textbf{m}}{m^{0}_{s}} has the following relationship with its corresponding stray field potential [3]:

Δ​U=d​i​v​(u​χΩ⁡(h)).\Delta U=div\left(\textbf{u}\chi_{\Omega(h)}\right).

For u∈H1​(Ω​(h))\textbf{u}\in H^{1}(\Omega(h)), U∈H˙1​(ℝ3)U\in\dot{H}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3}), in weak form this equation reads

∫ℝ3∇U⋅∇φ​𝑑x=∫Ω⁡(h)u⋅∇φ​𝑑x,∀φ∈C0∞​(ℝ3).\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\nabla U\cdot\nabla\varphi dx=\int_{\Omega(h)}\textbf{u}\cdot\nabla\varphi dx,\;\forall\varphi\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3}).\\ (1.2)

And the following inequality [6, 7] holds:

‖∇U‖Lp​(ℝ3)≤C​‖u‖Lp​(Ω​(h)),1<p<∞.\|\nabla U\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}\leq C\|\textbf{u}\|_{L^{p}(\Omega(h))},\quad 1<p<\infty.\\ (1.3)

For convenience of representation, we define the parameter symbols as follows:

L:=L1=L2,μ:=3​T5​(T−Tc),H:=He​f​f.L:=L_{1}=L_{2},\quad\mu:=\frac{3T}{5(T-T_{c})},\quad\textbf{H}:=\textbf{H}_{eff}.

From a×(b×c)=b⁡(a⋅c)−c⁡(a⋅b)a\times(b\times c)=b(a\cdot c)-c(a\cdot b), we have

u×(u×H)=(u⋅H)​u−|u|2​H.\textbf{u}\times(\textbf{u}\times\textbf{H})=(\textbf{u}\cdot\textbf{H})\textbf{u}-|\textbf{u}|^{2}\textbf{H}.

So equation (1.1) becomes

∂u∂t=γ​u×H+L​H=L⁡(A​Δ​u−∇U)+γ​u×(A​Δ​u−∇U)−Lχ11​(1+μ​|u|2)​u.\frac{\partial\textbf{u}}{\partial t}=\gamma\textbf{u}\times\textbf{H}+L\textbf{H}=L(A\Delta\textbf{u}-\nabla U)+\gamma\textbf{u}\times(A\Delta\textbf{u}-\nabla U)-\frac{L}{\chi_{11}}\left(1+\mu|\textbf{u}|^{2}\right)\textbf{u}. (1.4)

We proceed to adopt the dynamic mechanism in [19], assuming that energy is dominated by exchange energy, and considering the case of medium time scale and small damping, that is, for some ε>0\varepsilon>0 and a>0a>0

A⁡(h)h→ε,γ⁡(h)​h→1,L⁡(h)γ⁡(h)​h→a, as ​h→0.\frac{A(h)}{h}\rightarrow\varepsilon,\quad\gamma(h)\sqrt{h}\rightarrow 1,\quad\frac{L(h)}{\gamma(h)h}\rightarrow a,\text{ as }h\rightarrow 0.

The leading order energy effect of the stray field interaction in the film is a quadratic shape anisotropy conducive to in-plane magnetization, resulting in the formation of a forcing term pointing to the film plane and competing with the cyclotron force pushing the magnetization vector away from the plane [19]. Therefore, in the limit process (h→0h\rightarrow 0), some stray field energy will be converted into kinetic energy, and the limit spin polarization uu is planar.

LLB equation is developed from LL equation and LLG equation, but its form is more complex. The nonlinear term is increased from only involving the multiplication of two terms to three terms, which increases the influence on the interaction of stray field. More importantly, the favorable condition that the magnetization is constant is lost. First, the most direct impact is that the space of ut\textbf{u}_{t} is worse than L2L^{2} space, and some existing methods for L2L^{2} estimation can no longer be used. Secondly, when considering two important physical quantities in the vertical direction, if we still set w1h=1h​⨏0hu3​d​x3w_{1}^{h}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{h}}\fint_{0}^{h}u_{3}dx_{3} and w2h=1h​⨏0h∂U∂x3​d​x3w_{2}^{h}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{h}}\fint_{0}^{h}\frac{\partial U}{\partial x_{3}}dx_{3}, then the final limit equation will show singularity. So we have developed and improved some new methods and techniques. We add the square of spin polarization to w1hw_{1}^{h} and w2hw_{2}^{h} to avoid singularity, that is w1h=1h​⨏0h|u2|​u3​d​x3w_{1}^{h}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{h}}\fint_{0}^{h}\left|\textbf{u}^{2}\right|u_{3}dx_{3}, w2h=1h​⨏0h|u2|​∂U∂x3​d​x3w_{2}^{h}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{h}}\fint_{0}^{h}\left|\textbf{u}^{2}\right|\frac{\partial U}{\partial x_{3}}dx_{3}. This improvement produces many nonlinear terms involving the multiplication of three terms, which not only requires more and more precise estimates except L2L^{2}, but also requires higher space for strong convergence. In order to solve these problems, we extend the L2−L2L^{2}-L^{2} estimate on the average of product integrals to Lp−LqL^{p}-L^{q} estimate. And then we use Lp−LqL^{p}-L^{q} estimate, the energy methods and Gagliardo-Nirenberg interpolation to obtain more precise estimates of magnetization and stray field potential. Because the strong convergence space obtained by directly using the Compact Embedding Theorem in the past is poor, we combine the weak compactness argument with the Aubin-Lions Lemma to obtain the strong convergence in the better space. Finally, we derive the limit equation of LLB equation under the condition of appropriate compactness, and prove the limit process in a mathematically rigorous way.

∂uh∂t=γ​uh×H+L​H=:γ​uh×H¯+L​H,\frac{\partial\textbf{u}^{h}}{\partial t}=\gamma\textbf{u}^{h}\times\textbf{H}+L\textbf{H}=:\gamma\textbf{u}^{h}\times\bar{\textbf{H}}+L\textbf{H},

=∫0T∫Ω[u∧(ε​Δ′​u−∇′v)−β|u|2​u∧∂t2u]​ϕ​𝑑x​𝑑t=0,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\left[u\wedge(\varepsilon\Delta^{\prime}u-\nabla^{\prime}v)-\frac{\beta}{|u|^{2}}u\wedge\partial_{t}^{2}u\right]\phi dxdt=0,

where Δ′\Delta^{\prime} and ∇′\nabla^{\prime} represent Laplace operators and gradients of two-dimensional vectors, respectively. In order to avoid singularity, multiplying both sides of the equation by |u|2|u|^{2}, then the LLB limit equation formally reads

|u|2​u∧(ε​Δ′​u−∇′v)−β​u∧∂t2u=0.|u|^{2}u\wedge(\varepsilon\Delta^{\prime}u-\nabla^{\prime}v)-\beta u\wedge\partial_{t}^{2}u=0.

Under certain parameter mechanisms and assumptions, we will establish a three-dimensional model of LLB equation (1.4) on the film and study its initial boundary value problem. Thus, when the film thickness tends to zero, the limit equation is obtained and the limit process is proved in a mathematically rigorous way. The rest of the paper is arranged as follows. In Section 2, we will prove the existence of weak solutions of equation (1.4) considering the action of stray field (see Theorem 2.1), and then obtain the necessary compactness from the energy estimates. We also study the interaction of static magnetic field (stray field) without considering the setting of time variable, and get some lemmas. Finally, we state the main results of this paper (see Theorem 3.1) in Section 3, and prove main theorem in Section 4.

Given T>0T>0, a weak solution u:[0,T]→H1∩L4\textbf{u}:[0,T]\rightarrow H^{1}\cap L^{4} to (1.4) satisfies

The existence theorem of weak solution is given below.

Theorem 2.1.

Let ℬ⊂ℝ3\mathcal{B}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} be an open bounded domain with C2C^{2} boundary, for any given T>0T>0 and initial data u​(0)=u0∈H1\textbf{u}(0)=\textbf{u}_{0}\in H^{1}, there exists a weak solution of equation (1.4) such that u∈L∞​(0,T,H1)∩L2​(0,T,H2)\textbf{u}\in L^{\infty}(0,T;H^{1})\cap L^{2}(0,T;H^{2}).

Proof.

We use the Faedo-Galerkin approximation method to prove Theorem 2.1. Compared to [22], we consider an equation with the addition of the stray field. The method is the same, here we only give a brief proof.

According to [22], we find that approximate solution un∈Sn\textbf{u}_{n}\in S_{n} and Δ​un∈Sn\Delta\textbf{u}_{n}\in S_{n}. The induced stray field potential is UnU_{n} and ∇Un∈Sn\nabla U_{n}\in S_{n} by (1.3). Then we get

{∂un∂t−LAΔun+L∇Un−γAΠn(un×Δun)+γΠn(un×∇Un)+Lχ11Πn((1+μ|un|2)un)=0,un(x,0)=u0​n,u0​n∈Sn,\displaystyle\begin{cases}\frac{\partial\textbf{u}_{n}}{\partial t}-LA\Delta\textbf{u}_{n}+L\nabla U_{n}-\gamma A\Pi_{n}(\textbf{u}_{n}\times\Delta\textbf{u}_{n})+\gamma\Pi_{n}(\textbf{u}_{n}\times\nabla U_{n})+\frac{L}{\chi_{11}}\Pi_{n}\left(\left(1+\mu|\textbf{u}_{n}|^{2}\right)\textbf{u}_{n}\right)=0,\\ \textbf{u}_{n}(x,0)=\textbf{u}_{0n},\quad\textbf{u}_{0n}\in S_{n},\end{cases} (2.2)

and

≤‖u1×(∇U1−∇U2)‖L2+‖(u1−u2)×∇U2‖L2\displaystyle\leq\|\textbf{u}_{1}\times(\nabla U_{1}-\nabla U_{2})\|_{L^{2}}+\|(\textbf{u}_{1}-\textbf{u}_{2})\times\nabla U_{2}\|_{L^{2}}
≤‖u1‖L∞​‖∇U1−∇U2‖L2+‖u1−u2‖L2​‖∇U2‖L∞\displaystyle\leq\|\textbf{u}_{1}\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\nabla U_{1}-\nabla U_{2}\|_{L^{2}}+\|\textbf{u}_{1}-\textbf{u}_{2}\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla U_{2}\|_{L^{\infty}}
≤C​‖u1‖L∞​‖u1−u2‖L2+‖u1−u2‖L2​‖∇U2‖L∞.\displaystyle\leq C\|\textbf{u}_{1}\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\textbf{u}_{1}-\textbf{u}_{2}\|_{L^{2}}+\|\textbf{u}_{1}-\textbf{u}_{2}\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla U_{2}\|_{L^{\infty}}.

By using the existence theorem of solutions of the ordinary differential equations, we can obtain the existence of approximate solutions. From (2.2), we can easily establish the following estimates:

According to Hölder’s inequality, (2.3), and (2.4), we have

There exist a subsequence of {Πn​(un×∇Un)}\{\Pi_{n}(\textbf{u}_{n}\times\nabla U_{n})\} (still denoted by {Πn​(un×∇Un)}\{\Pi_{n}(\textbf{u}_{n}\times\nabla U_{n})\}) and Z¯∈L2​(0,T,X−β)\bar{Z}\in L^{2}(0,T;X^{-\beta}), such that

To study the interaction of stray field on thin magnet in simple environment, only electrostatic magnetic field needs to be considered. At the end of this section, we give some lemmas of stray field interaction without considering time variables.

Considering electrostatic magnetic field

uh:Ω⁡(h)→ℝ3,uh∈H1​(Ω⁡(h)),\textbf{u}^{h}:~\Omega(h)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3},\quad\textbf{u}^{h}\in H^{1}(\Omega(h)),

by Hölder’s inequality and the G-N inequality, one has uh∈Lp​(Ω⁡(h))\textbf{u}^{h}\in L^{p}(\Omega(h)) for 1≤p≤61\leq p\leq 6.

From the potential equation Δ​Uh=d​i​v​(uh​χΩ⁡(h))\Delta U^{h}=div(\textbf{u}^{h}\chi_{\Omega(h)}), its unique solution Uh∈H˙1​(ℝ3)U^{h}\in\dot{H}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) satisfies

∫ℝ3∇Uh⋅∇ϕ​𝑑x=∫Ω⁡(h)uh⋅∇ϕ​𝑑x,ϕ∈H˙1​(ℝ3).\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\nabla U^{h}\cdot\nabla\phi dx=\int_{\Omega(h)}\textbf{u}^{h}\cdot\nabla\phi dx,\quad\phi\in\dot{H}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3}). (2.11)

And according to (1.3), we have

‖∇Uh‖L6​(ℝ3)≲‖uh‖L6​(Ω​(h))<∞,\left\|\nabla U^{h}\right\|_{L^{6}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}\lesssim\left\|\textbf{u}^{h}\right\|_{L^{6}(\Omega(h))}<\infty,

which yields that the weak form of potential equation can be also written as

∫ℝ3∇Uh⋅∇ϕ​𝑑x=∫Ω⁡(h)uh⋅∇ϕ​𝑑x,ϕ∈W1,65​(ℝ3).\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\nabla U^{h}\cdot\nabla\phi dx=\int_{\Omega(h)}\textbf{u}^{h}\cdot\nabla\phi dx,\quad\phi\in W^{1,\frac{6}{5}}(\mathbb{R}^{3}). (2.12)

Noticing that ∇ϕ∈L65​(ℝ3)\nabla\phi\in L^{\frac{6}{5}}(\mathbb{R}^{3}), and we can naturally obtain ϕ∈L2​(ℝ3)\phi\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) by the G-N inequality.

In order to determine the asymptotic limit, two important physical quantities in the vertical direction are defined by

w1h=1h​⨏0h|uh|2​u3h​d​x3,w2h=1h​⨏0h|uh|2​∂Uh∂x3​d​x3.w_{1}^{h}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{h}}\fint_{0}^{h}\left|\textbf{u}^{h}\right|^{2}u_{3}^{h}dx_{3},\quad w_{2}^{h}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{h}}\fint_{0}^{h}\left|\textbf{u}^{h}\right|^{2}\frac{\partial U^{h}}{\partial x_{3}}dx_{3}.

|∫Ω(⨏0h(f⋅g)−⨏0hf​⨏0hg)​𝑑x|≤h​(⨏Ω⁡(h)|∂f∂x3|p​𝑑x)1p​(⨏Ω⁡(h)|g|q​𝑑x)1q,\left|\int_{\Omega}\left(\fint_{0}^{h}(f\cdot g)-\fint_{0}^{h}f\fint_{0}^{h}g\right)dx\right|\leq h\left(\fint_{\Omega(h)}\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{3}}\right|^{p}dx\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}\left(\fint_{\Omega(h)}|g|^{q}dx\right)^{\frac{1}{q}},

where 1p+1q=1\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=1, 1<p1<p, q<∞.q<\infty.

According to Lemma 2.4 in [19], we have

⨏0h(f⋅g)​d​x3−⨏0hf​d​x3⋅⨏0hg​d​x3=⨏0h⨏0h(∫z2z1∂f∂x3​(x,y)​𝑑y)​g​(x,z1)​d​z1​d​z2.\fint_{0}^{h}(f\cdot g)dx_{3}-\fint_{0}^{h}fdx_{3}\cdot\fint_{0}^{h}gdx_{3}=\fint_{0}^{h}\fint_{0}^{h}\left(\int_{z_{2}}^{z_{1}}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{3}}(x,y)dy\right)g(x,z_{1})dz_{1}dz_{2}.

Using Hölder’s inequality, we calculate

|∫Ω(⨏0h(f⋅g)​d​x3−⨏0hf​d​x3⋅⨏0hg​d​x3)​𝑑x|=|∫Ω⨏0h⨏0h(∫z2z1∂f∂x3​(x,y)​𝑑y)​g​(x,z1)​d​z1​d​z2​𝑑x|\displaystyle\quad\left|\int_{\Omega}\left(\fint_{0}^{h}\!(f\cdot g)dx_{3}-\fint_{0}^{h}\!fdx_{3}\cdot\fint_{0}^{h}\!gdx_{3}\right)dx\right|\!=\!\left|\int_{\Omega}\fint_{0}^{h}\!\!\fint_{0}^{h}\!\!\left(\int_{z_{2}}^{z_{1}}\!\!\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{3}}(x,y)dy\right)g(x,z_{1})dz_{1}dz_{2}dx\right|
=|∫Ω⨏0h⨏0h(∫0h∂f∂x3​(x,y)​d​z2)​g​(x,z1)​d​z1​𝑑y​𝑑x|≤h​∫Ω⨏0h⨏0h|∂f∂x3​(x,y)|​|g⁡(x,z1)|​𝑑y​d​z1​𝑑x\displaystyle=\left|\int_{\Omega}\fint_{0}^{h}\fint_{0}^{h}\left(\int_{0}^{h}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{3}}(x,y)dz_{2}\right)g(x,z_{1})dz_{1}dydx\right|\leq h\int_{\Omega}\fint_{0}^{h}\fint_{0}^{h}\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{3}}(x,y)\right|\left|g(x,z_{1})\right|dydz_{1}dx
=h​∫Ω(⨏0h|∂f∂x3​(x,y)|​𝑑y)​(⨏0h|g⁡(x,z1)|​d​z1)​𝑑x≤h​(⨏Ω⁡(h)|∂f∂x3|p​𝑑x)1p​(⨏Ω⁡(h)|g|q​𝑑x)1q.\displaystyle=h\int_{\Omega}\left(\fint_{0}^{h}\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{3}}(x,y)\right|dy\right)\left(\fint_{0}^{h}\left|g(x,z_{1})\right|dz_{1}\right)dx\leq h\left(\fint_{\Omega(h)}\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{3}}\right|^{p}dx\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}\left(\fint_{\Omega(h)}\left|g\right|^{q}dx\right)^{\frac{1}{q}}.

Lemma 2.7.

If

vh⇀v​ in ​H˙1​(ℝ3),⨏0huh​d​x3⇀(u,0)​ in ​L2​(Ω),v^{h}\rightharpoonup v\text{ in }\dot{H}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3}),\;\,\fint_{0}^{h}\textbf{u}^{h}dx_{3}\rightharpoonup(u,0)\text{ in }L^{2}(\Omega),

while h​∫Ω⁡(h)|∂uh∂x3|2​𝑑x→0h\int_{\Omega(h)}\left|\frac{\partial\textbf{u}^{h}}{\partial x_{3}}\right|^{2}dx\rightarrow 0, then vv is a weak solution of the following equation:

∫ℝ3∇v⋅∇φdx=∫Ωu(x)∇φ(x,0)dx,∀φ∈C0∞(ℝ3).\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\nabla v\cdot\nabla\varphi dx=\int_{\Omega}u(x)\nabla\varphi(x,0)dx,\ \ \forall\varphi\in C^{\infty}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{3}).

Finally, we prove the regularity of the time derivative of the stray field induced by the magnetization field uh=uh​(t)\textbf{u}^{h}=\textbf{u}^{h}(t).

Lemma 2.8.

If suph∫0∞(⨏Ω⁡(h)|uth|32​𝑑x)43​𝑑t<∞\sup\limits_{h}\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(\fint_{\Omega(h)}\left|\textbf{u}_{t}^{h}\right|^{\frac{3}{2}}dx\right)^{\frac{4}{3}}dt<\infty, then vthv_{t}^{h} is uniformly bounded about hh in L2​(ℝ3×(0,∞))L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\times(0,\infty)).

Proof.

Let ψ∈C0∞​(ℝ3×(0,∞))\psi\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\times(0,\infty)) and |ψ|≥1|\psi|\geq 1. Then the associated Newton potential φ∈C∞​(ℝ3×(0,∞))\varphi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\times(0,\infty)) solving Δ​φ​(⋅,t)=ψ⁡(⋅,t)\Delta\varphi(\cdot,t)=\psi(\cdot,t) is compactly supported in time (see [30]). Since Δ​φt=ψt\Delta\varphi_{t}=\psi_{t}, we have

∫0T⨏Ω⁡(h)u1h​∂vh∂x2​|uh|2​ϕ​𝑑x​𝑑t→∫0T∫Ω⨏0hu1h​d​x3⋅⨏0h∂vh∂x2​|uh|2​ϕ​d​x3​𝑑x​𝑑t.\int_{0}^{T}\fint_{\Omega(h)}u_{1}^{h}\frac{\partial v^{h}}{\partial x_{2}}\left|\textbf{u}^{h}\right|^{2}\phi dxdt\rightarrow\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\fint_{0}^{h}u_{1}^{h}dx_{3}\cdot\fint_{0}^{h}\frac{\partial v^{h}}{\partial x_{2}}\left|\textbf{u}^{h}\right|^{2}\phi dx_{3}dxdt.

Similarly, by Lemma 2.6, Hölder’s inequality, (3.9), (3.10) and (3.12), we get

|∫0T∫Ω(⨏0h∂vh∂x2​|uh|2​d​x3−⨏0h∂vh∂x2​d​x3⋅⨏0h|uh|2​d​x3)​𝑑x​𝑑t|\displaystyle\quad\left|\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\left(\fint_{0}^{h}\frac{\partial v^{h}}{\partial x_{2}}\left|\textbf{u}^{h}\right|^{2}dx_{3}-\fint_{0}^{h}\frac{\partial v^{h}}{\partial x_{2}}dx_{3}\cdot\fint_{0}^{h}\left|\textbf{u}^{h}\right|^{2}dx_{3}\right)dxdt\right|
≲h​(∫0T∫ℝ3|∂vh∂x2|2​𝑑x​𝑑t)12​supt(⨏Ω⁡(h)|uh|6​𝑑x)16​[∫0T(⨏Ω⁡(h)|∂uh∂x3|3​𝑑x)23​𝑑t]12→0.\displaystyle\lesssim\sqrt{h}\left(\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\left|\frac{\partial v^{h}}{\partial x_{2}}\right|^{2}dxdt\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\sup\limits_{t}\left(\fint_{\Omega(h)}\left|\textbf{u}^{h}\right|^{6}dx\right)^{\frac{1}{6}}\left[\int_{0}^{T}\left(\fint_{\Omega(h)}\left|\frac{\partial\textbf{u}^{h}}{\partial x_{3}}\right|^{3}dx\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}dt\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}\rightarrow 0.

Then

∫0T⨏Ω⁡(h)∂vh∂x2​|uh|2​d​x3​𝑑x​𝑑t→∫0T∫Ω⨏0h∂vh∂x2​d​x3⋅⨏0h|uh|2​d​x3​𝑑x​𝑑t.\int_{0}^{T}\fint_{\Omega(h)}\frac{\partial v^{h}}{\partial x_{2}}\left|\textbf{u}^{h}\right|^{2}dx_{3}dxdt\rightarrow\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\fint_{0}^{h}\frac{\partial v^{h}}{\partial x_{2}}dx_{3}\cdot\fint_{0}^{h}\left|\textbf{u}^{h}\right|^{2}dx_{3}dxdt.

Now, we prove

⨏0h∇vhdx3⇀∇v(x1,x2,0,t) in L2(0,T;L2(Ω)).\displaystyle\fint_{0}^{h}\nabla v^{h}dx_{3}\rightharpoonup\nabla v(x_{1},x_{2},0,t)\text{ in }L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega)). (4.15)

It follows from Hölder’s inequality and (3.9) that ⨏0h∇vhdx3\fint_{0}^{h}\nabla v^{h}dx_{3} is uniformly bounded in L2​(0,T,L2​(Ω))L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega)). Then ⨏0h∇vhdx3\fint_{0}^{h}\nabla v^{h}dx_{3} weakly converges in L2​(0,T,L2​(Ω))L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega)) by the weak compactness argument. From Proposition 4.2 in [19], we deduce ⨏0hvh​d​x3→v⁡(x1,x2,0,t)​ in ​L2​(0,T,L2​(Ω))\fint_{0}^{h}v^{h}dx_{3}\rightarrow v(x_{1},x_{2},0,t)\text{ in }L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega)). By the fact that L2​(Ω×(0,T))⊂H−1​(Ω×(0,T))L^{2}(\Omega\times(0,T))\subset H^{-1}(\Omega\times(0,T)), we infer that ⨏0h∇vhdx3\fint_{0}^{h}\nabla v^{h}dx_{3} weakly converges in H−1​(Ω×(0,T))H^{-1}(\Omega\times(0,T)). Then for any ψ∈H01​(Ω×(0,T))\psi\in H_{0}^{1}(\Omega\times(0,T)), we have

∫0T∫Ω⨏0h∇vhdx3⋅ψdxdt=−∫0T∫Ω⨏0hvhdx3⋅∇ψdxdt\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\fint_{0}^{h}\nabla v^{h}dx_{3}\cdot\psi dxdt=-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\fint_{0}^{h}v^{h}dx_{3}\cdot\nabla\psi dxdt
→−∫0T∫Ωv(x1,x2,0,t)⋅∇ψdxdt=∫0T∫Ω∇v(x1,x2,0,t)⋅ψdxdt,\displaystyle\rightarrow-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}v(x_{1},x_{2},0,t)\cdot\nabla\psi dxdt=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\nabla v(x_{1},x_{2},0,t)\cdot\psi dxdt,

thus (4.15) holds by the uniqueness of the limit. This combined with (4.12) yields that

⨏0h∂vh∂x2​|uh|2​d​x3⇀∂v∂x2​|u|2​ in ​L65​(0,T,L65​(Ω)).\fint_{0}^{h}\frac{\partial v^{h}}{\partial x_{2}}\left|\textbf{u}^{h}\right|^{2}dx_{3}\rightharpoonup\frac{\partial v}{\partial x_{2}}|\textbf{u}|^{2}\text{ in }L^{\frac{6}{5}}(0,T;L^{\frac{6}{5}}(\Omega)).

It follows from (4.9) that

∫0T⨏Ω⁡(h)u1h​∂vh∂x2​|uh|2​ϕ​𝑑x​𝑑t→∫0T∫Ωu1​∂v∂x2​|u|2​ϕ​𝑑x​𝑑t.\int_{0}^{T}\fint_{\Omega(h)}u_{1}^{h}\frac{\partial v^{h}}{\partial x_{2}}\left|\textbf{u}^{h}\right|^{2}\phi dxdt\rightarrow\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}u_{1}\frac{\partial v}{\partial x_{2}}|\textbf{u}|^{2}\phi dxdt.

Similarly,

∫0T⨏Ω⁡(h)u2h​∂vh∂x1​|uh|2​ϕ​𝑑x​𝑑t→∫0T∫Ωu2​∂v∂x1​|u|2​ϕ​𝑑x​𝑑t.\int_{0}^{T}\fint_{\Omega(h)}u_{2}^{h}\frac{\partial v^{h}}{\partial x_{1}}\left|\textbf{u}^{h}\right|^{2}\phi dxdt\rightarrow\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}u_{2}\frac{\partial v}{\partial x_{1}}|\textbf{u}|^{2}\phi dxdt.

Therefore, (4.14) is proved by |u|2=|u|2|\textbf{u}|^{2}=|u|^{2}, then (4.7) holds. The conclusion of Step 2 is proved. Combining the conclusions of Step 1 and Step 2, the proof of Proposition 4.2 is completed. ∎

Finally, we use Proposition 4.1 and Proposition 4.2 to derive the limit equation (3.16).

Proof.

From Lemma 2.5 and Proposition 4.1, we have

w1h⇀u∧ut​ in ​L2​(0,T,L65​(Ω)).w_{1}^{h}\rightharpoonup u\wedge u_{t}\text{ in }L^{2}(0,T;L^{\frac{6}{5}}(\Omega)).

This combined with Proposition 4.2 yields that

∫0T∫Ωw1h⋅ϕt+∂tw1h⋅ϕ​𝑑x​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}w_{1}^{h}\cdot\phi_{t}+\partial_{t}w_{1}^{h}\cdot\phi dxdt →∫0T∫Ωu∧ut⋅ϕt+|u|2​[∇′(u∧∇′u)−u∧∇′v]⋅ϕ​𝑑x​𝑑t\displaystyle\rightarrow\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}u\wedge u_{t}\cdot\phi_{t}+|u|^{2}\left[\nabla^{\prime}\left(u\wedge\nabla^{\prime}u\right)-u\wedge\nabla^{\prime}v\right]\cdot\phi dxdt
=∫0T∫Ω−u∧ut​t⋅ϕ+|u|2[∇′(u∧∇′u)−u∧∇′v]⋅ϕdxdt\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}-u\wedge u_{tt}\cdot\phi+|u|^{2}\left[\nabla^{\prime}\left(u\wedge\nabla^{\prime}u\right)-u\wedge\nabla^{\prime}v\right]\cdot\phi dxdt
=−∫0T∫Ωu∧(ut​t−|u|2Δ′u+|u|2∇′v)⋅ϕdxdt.\displaystyle=-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}u\wedge\left(u_{tt}-|u|^{2}\Delta^{\prime}u+|u|^{2}\nabla^{\prime}v\right)\cdot\phi dxdt.

Since

∫0T∫Ωw1h⋅ϕt+∂tw1h⋅ϕ​𝑑x​𝑑t=∫0T∫Ωw1h​ϕt−w1h⋅ϕt​𝑑x​𝑑t=0,\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}w_{1}^{h}\cdot\phi_{t}+\partial_{t}w_{1}^{h}\cdot\phi dxdt=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}w_{1}^{h}\phi_{t}-w_{1}^{h}\cdot\phi_{t}dxdt=0,

then

∫0T∫Ωu∧(ut​t−|u|2​Δ′​u+|u|2​∇′v)⋅ϕ​𝑑x​𝑑t=0.\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}u\wedge\left(u_{tt}-|u|^{2}\Delta^{\prime}u+|u|^{2}\nabla^{\prime}v\right)\cdot\phi dxdt=0.

We get the desired results. The proof of Theorem 3.1 is completed. ∎
